stem: A stroke program tracks door-to-needle (DTN) time for clients receiving intravenous thrombolysis. What does this metric measure?

options.A: The interval from hospital arrival to initiation of intravenous thrombolytic treatment.
options.B: The interval from symptom onset to hospital arrival, which is an onset-to-door metric rather than DTN.
options.C: The interval from thrombolytic administration to hospital discharge.
options.D: The interval from hospital arrival to completion of post-stroke rehabilitation.

rationale: A is correct. AHA/ASA Target: Stroke uses door-to-needle time to measure how quickly eligible acute ischemic stroke patients receive intravenous thrombolysis after arriving at the hospital. Current AHA/ASA guidance emphasizes rapid treatment because thrombolytic benefit is time dependent. B describes prehospital delay rather than DTN. C and D occur after thrombolysis and are not door-to-needle measures.
educational_objective: Interpret door-to-needle time as the hospital-arrival-to-IV-thrombolysis interval and recognize it as a stroke quality-improvement metric used to reduce in-hospital treatment delay.
source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
source_document_title: Target: Stroke — Learn More About Target: Stroke; 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
source_version_date: Current Target: Stroke page and 2026 AIS guideline accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Target: Stroke: quality-improvement initiative focused on reducing door-to-needle times for eligible acute ischemic stroke patients treated with IV thrombolysis; performance goals are expressed as treatment within specified minutes of hospital arrival. 2026 AIS Guideline: hospitals and stroke systems should track time metrics and initiate IV thrombolysis as quickly as possible in eligible patients.
source_claim_supported: Door-to-needle time is the interval from hospital arrival to initiation of IV thrombolysis and is used as a stroke-care quality metric to identify and reduce treatment delays.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: participate in performance improvement and quality-improvement processes and coordinate time-sensitive care.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — stroke door-to-needle quality metric
correction_summary: Corrected the blueprint from Safety & Infection Prevention and Control to Management of Care and rebuilt the item around the precise quality-metric definition. Avoided implying that a single historic DTN threshold is the only acceptable current quality target; the construct is the arrival-to-treatment interval and minimizing delay.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current AHA Target: Stroke material and the 2026 AHA/ASA AIS guideline.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A is the DTN definition. B is onset-to-door. C and D are post-treatment intervals.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; hospital arrival to IV thrombolysis.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; rehabilitation timing is unrelated to DTN.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A defines DTN; no drug-specific wording is required because the metric applies to IV thrombolytic treatment.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are time intervals in the stroke-care pathway.
audit_findings.blueprint: Quality-improvement measurement fits Management of Care.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked historical tPA-specific terminology versus current alteplase/tenecteplase IVT practice. The final item uses IV thrombolysis generically while preserving the established DTN definition. No second answer remained.
